questions.explanation: Half of group A's qualified applicants are wrongly rejected, 10 of 20, while only 2 of 20 is 1 in 10 for group B, so group A carries five times the share of the harm. Group size alone does not decide this, and equal numbers of qualified people can still mean very different rejection rates. Comparing totals instead of rates points at the wrong group entirely.

questions.explanation: Both flagged cases are truly qualified, so no false positive occurs, and of the four unflagged cases two are truly qualified, giving 2 false negatives, which means two qualified people are wrongly cleared. Swapping the two labels would say the opposite, and the four unflagged rows are not four false positives, because two of them are correctly unflagged. Case order never changes which count moves.
questions.hint: Compare each row's flag with its true state, one row at a time.

questions.stem: Trace this audit and report the false positives and false negatives. flagged <- [yes, yes, no, no, no, no]. truth <- [yes, yes, yes, yes, no, no]. fp <- 0. fn <- 0. FOR EACH i FROM 1 TO 6 { IF flagged[i] = yes { IF truth[i] = no { fp <- fp + 1 } } ELSE { IF truth[i] = yes { fn <- fn + 1 } } } DISPLAY fp, fn

questions.explanation: Group A misses 4 of its 100 qualified applicants, which is 4 percent, and group B misses 30 of 100, which is 30 percent, so the gap is 30 minus 4, or 26 percentage points. Dividing 30 by 4 compares the two rates instead of taking the difference, and adding them gives 34 points, which is not a gap. The units are percentage points because both rates use the same denominator of 100.
questions.hint: Both rates use a denominator of 100, so the gap is a plain subtraction.
questions.learningObjective: compute the percentage-point gap between two error rates

answer.exemplar: The system's own output becomes its next input: it recommends only to people already playing daily, those people keep playing, and the quiet listeners are never shown anything that might suit them, so they never appear as candidates either. Break the loop by reserving a fixed share of slots, or a randomised exploration slot, for people outside the current audience, then check whether the engagement gap between groups actually narrows.

questions.explanation: A model fed only on past behaviour cannot discover preferences it has never been shown, so each cycle confirms the last one and the app reports healthy engagement for the group it already reaches. Deliberately sampling newcomers, and watching the outcome for groups the model rarely serves, is what stops the system's own history being mistaken for the world's preferences.
questions.hint: Ask who is never shown anything, and why that keeps them invisible.
